This paper introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel econometric framework designed for modeling and forecasting count time series. We demonstrate that the score-driven approach is ideal for tracking the evolution of time-varying parameters, offering the necessary flexibility to handle count data with complex nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks. Under mild conditions, we establish the asymptotic properties of the TV-PARX model, proving that maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) produces parameter estimates that are both strongly consistent and asymptotically normal. Monte Carlo simulations are used to assess finite-sample performance and forecasting precision. Furthermore, the practical value of the TV-PARX model's time-varying specification is illustrated through an analysis of daily new COVID-19 infections in Italy and corporate defaults in the United States. To facilitate adoption, we have made the implementation of both the TV-PARX model and its asymptotic theory accessible through the R package 'dynamicparx' (available at https://github.com/countdata/dynamicparx). This work extends the asymptotic analysis originally developed by Kalyankrishna and Shephard (2019) to accommodate count time series data.
Although the concept of employing stellar photometry to monitor the atmosphere for high-energy astrophysics optical experiments appears simple, achieving the high precision required to determine vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) to within 0.01 has been challenging. Wide-field photometry spanning various altitudes enables a rapid, calibration-independent VAOD calculation, while simultaneously serving as a valuable calibration by-product. By leveraging multi-year datasets from the FRAM (F/(Ph)otometric Robotic Atmospheric Monitor) telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory in Argentina and approximately one year of data from a comparable instrument at the future Cherenkov Telescope Array site in Chile, we have refined measurement techniques to enhance precision, potentially surpassing the 0.01 threshold. Crucially, this analysis relied on detailed laboratory assessments of the system's response to light spectrum and intensity, as the standard assumption of CCD detector linearity no longer holds under these specific observational conditions. Utilizing a rigorous error propagation framework, we identified several previously unrecognized sources of uncertainty, which, when incorporated, resulted in a precise and calibration-independent VAOD measurement of 0.02 over a range of 0.1 to 2.8, utilizing a newly developed, broader-bandpass filter designed to minimize dependence on assumptions regarding the atmospheric aerosol spectral characteristics. Detailed methodologies, the calibrated best-fit parameters for this VAOD-sky brightness relationship, and the complete uncalibrated datasets suitable for re-analysis at the time of deployment for the Cherenkov Telescope Array are documented in this report and accessible via the accompanying video.

These could involve comparing systems on their ability to prioritize information in accessibly described images or conducting user studies to determine which systems produce descriptions that users find more natural and useful. Ultimately, the quality of reference data remains crucial; however, we must also consider how to evaluate systems when such gold-standard data is available but limited in scope.

This section examines predictions from the bilepton model, an extension of the standard model where the gauge group shifts from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3) \times U(1)$ and fermion families are arranged non-sequentially, with the third family differing from the first two. To satisfy the requirements for triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom, the model necessitates exactly three families. The anticipated new physics comprises bileptons and three heavy quarks, ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. While QCD will bind these heavy quarks with light quarks and among themselves to create baryons and mesons, these composite particles will remain undetectable at the LHC but could be observed at a hypothetical 100 TeV proton-proton collider, unlike the bileptons. Given that the three-light-heavy quarks would behave similarly to the heavy top quark within the standard model, one might anticipate 2-1-1 ratios for baryon-to-meson production of the ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$ quarks. However, flavor $SU(3)$ symmetry must be invoked for the three heavy quarks to explain their comparable production rates. We will examine the masses and production ratios of the bileptons and the ${\cal D}$${\cal T}$ meson at a 100 TeV collider. Additionally, we will consider the decay of the ${\cal T}$Q baryon (where Q represents any up- or down-type quark), which will manifest as a characteristic signature at a 100 TeV proton-proton collider. Finally, we will address why nature selected $SU(3) \times U(1)$ over other possible gauge groups like $SU(N)$ for the weak force, and why the third family of fermions was assigned different quantum numbers under $SU(3) \times U(1)$ compared to the first two families.
This paper introduces IDET systems grounded in SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM, serving as the counterparts to our optimal wideband waveforming approach detailed in [1]. We formulate optimization problems aimed at maximizing both fair-throughput and sum-throughput. Leveraging a fixed-point based alternating algorithm, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput solutions for both SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM configurations. We demonstrate that the optimal fair-throughput solution aligns with the most recent SISO single-stream solution found in literature, whereas the optimal sum-throughput solution for MISO-OFDM exceeds those achievable by SISO single-stream, multi-stream, and wideband solutions. The benefits of SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM are highlighted through specific application scenarios. Numerical examples focus on a two-user setup, comparing these solutions against time-switching (TS) based protocols, confirming the superiority of IDET systems; specifically, IFU-OFDM and IDU-MOFDM achieve infinite transmission time ratios ($\alpha$) whereas TS protocols do not. Additionally, we establish that IDU-MOFDM outperforms IFU-OFDM in terms of throughput, a conclusion verified in the numerical analysis. Finally, the advantages of wideband solutions over OFDM solutions are illustrated by specific use-case examples within the numerical study. Fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) demands a unified framework that integrates extensive datasets from both theoretical predictions and experimental data. While data integration primarily involves standardizing formats, incorporating theoretical predictions is more complex due to the involvement of multiple components. Various independent groups develop distinct providers for different processes, utilizing diverse input parameters (runcards) and output structures (interpolation grids). Furthermore, because processes are measured across different scales, the PDF candidate requires DGLAP evolution, either calculated dynamically or precomputed into grids. Our goal is to automate all these steps within a single framework, making it a valuable resource for any PDF fitting group and potentially for broader phenomenological investigations. To achieve this, we have created a Python library called Amelia (Automated Ellison Method for Analysis), which serves as the counterpart to Madam for fitting Parton Shower parameters. This abstract outlines the necessary components for this endeavor and explains how we have implemented them in Amelia; the library's modular design allows for easy replacement of components should better options become available. Fortunately, most components are group-independent, with the Distribution Grid being the most significant specialized element. We have developed a set of routines to load, resample, and interpolate Cubic Spline grids, which form the foundation of all modern PDF sets. These routines ensure that groups only need to provide the raw grid files, while the remainder of the setup remains consistent. Other elements, such as runcards and process implementations, vary based on the specific fit being performed. We detail how we constructed an implementation for V(n) cross sections (including Drell Yan, Photon + Jet, Z + Jet, and Top Antitop), utilizing Madgraph5_auto [1] as the computational engine, with our code managing dynamical masses, scale choices, and spin-1 PDF assignment. For other processes, we recommend connecting to an external implementation via a routine that specifies the process name, its ID, and the desired output type (spline or dynamic dynamic). Finally, we demonstrate the complete workflow by fitting a modern PDF set and a Dragon shower parameter, utilizing a dataset from the ATLAS V(n) measurement [2].

This research conducts a linear analysis of a turbulent methane-air jet flame to forecast how the reacting flow responds to upstream acoustic actuation. Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them ideal for this application. These RANS models were linearized around the temporal mean flow of the turbulent jet, which was derived using LES. An a priori analysis identified the linearized RANS-Eddy Break Up (EBU) model as the most appropriate choice for the specific setup, demonstrating high accuracy in reproducing LES-derived reaction rate fluctuations. Subsequently, the linearized governing equations, including the linearized EBU model for reaction rates, were solved for incoming acoustic perturbations. The resulting response modes indicate that reaction rate oscillations stem from Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings disturbing the jet flame. These findings align well with LES simulations regarding the mode shapes of both velocity and reaction rate fluctuations. Ultimately, this a priori analysis confirms that the linearized RANS-EBU model accurately represents reaction rate fluctuations in this scenario, offering a computationally efficient alternative to LES for such analyses.
Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a classical, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal components of the constitutive relation directly link measurable quantities, mirroring the approach found in nonlocal electrodynamics. The derived constitutive relation aligns with a recent proposal by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25]. Utilizing this updated constitutive relation for NLG, it is demonstrated that de Sitter spacetime does not constitute a valid solution. Furthermore, the constitutive relation is optimized to ensure compatibility with post-Newtonian expansions. Finally, it is proven that the complete constitutive relation, and consequently the nonlocal field equations themselves, lack a well-defined asymptotic expansion with respect to the causal kernel. These findings regarding the constitutive relation have significant implications for the constitutive ocant of NLG, potentially guiding future research directions. Notably, these conclusions stand in direct contrast to a recent claim by S. Ghosh [10], asserting that the constitutive relation proposed by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl is equivalent to a well-defined second-order differential relation among dynamical variables; this paper provides a proof showing that such an equivalence cannot exist. The work relies heavily on the optical representation of Spacetime, Finsler geometry, and the theory of nonlocal functions on Spacetime, particularly Bochner's representation formula. Additionally, concepts from information theory are employed to justify the choice of the causal kernel.

The detection of certain variable X-ray sources in the Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over a ten-year monitoring period has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. However, this paper demonstrates that approximately half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade when observed with MAXI sensitivity. Furthermore, we show that to align the expected total number of neutron star LMXBs with both current observations and the galaxy's millisecond radio pulsar population, the dominant class of these systems must have recurrence times far surpassing a century for MAXI-detectable outbursts, implying that few such systems have been identified to date. Finally, we argue that future searches for transient LMXBs using Chandra, which employ much lower threshold fluxes than MAXI, are essential for accurately determining the total population of these systems.
Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two separate sets of entities. These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. We demonstrate that deciding whether a planar drawing is achievable by splitting at most $k$ vertices is fixed parameter tractable with respect to $k$. Furthermore, we provide an algorithm capable of producing a planar visualization by splitting up to $k$ vertices, whose runtime does not depend exponentially on the graph's partition size. Finally, we describe an approach for approximating the optimal set of split vertices for larger values of $k$, and we outline methods to extend these techniques to multiple instances. To conclude, we discuss the relevance of these findings by applying them to real-world datasets. The body of this paper focuses on a progressive reduction of visualizations, specifically targeting the elimination of edge crossings. We redefined the problem of determining a planar drawing by allowing vertices to be split into multiple copies, ensuring that all edges connecting a given vertex instance to its duplicates form a planar subgraph. By defining a split set as a group of vertices where every pair is connected by a path that uses only edges incident to at least one vertex in the set, we established that there exists a planar drawing with the above mentioned property if and only if the corresponding split set can be made planar. Additionally, we confirmed that minimizing crossings remains fixed parameter tractable when optimized around this split set, ultimately resulting in a planar visualization where all vertices are split. For empirical data, we outlined an algorithm to identify a split set of size at most $k$ that admits a crossing-free drawing, and we detailed how to compute an optimal crossing-free drawing for every vertex in this set. Finally, we addressed the challenge of approximating the size of an optimal split set for real dataset visualizations. Regarding future research directions, we noted that for general graphs, determining whether a planar drawing exists by splitting at most $k$ vertices is feasible, although calculating the exact set of vertices to split remains an open issue. Performance degradation techniques serve as a crucial complement to side-channel attacks. This study introduces HyperDegrade, a novel method that integrates prior strategies with simultaneous multithreading (SMT) architectures. Beyond this new technique, we identify a previously unrecognized source of slowdown by analyzing cache eviction as a root cause. The resulting performance degradation is substantially greater than previous methods, thereby enhancing the time granularity available for Flush+Reload attacks. We evaluated HyperDegrade across various Intel microarchitectures, achieving significant slowdowns that, in specific microbenchmark scenarios, represent a three-order-of-magnitude improvement over state-of-the-art solutions. To assess the effectiveness of performance degradation in amplifying side channels, we introduced and validated specific leakage metrics. Our findings indicate that HyperDegrade improves time granularity without compromising trace quality. Furthermore, we conducted a fair comparison of three performance degradation strategies when paired with Flush+Reload from an attacker's viewpoint. We also devised an attack targeting an underutilized vulnerability in OpenSSL, where HyperDegrade demonstrated superior performance by reducing the number of required Flush+Reload traces needed for success by a factor of three. In terms of cryptographic contributions, we revisited the recently proposed Raccoon attack on TLS-DH key exchanges, extending its application to other protocols. Leveraging HyperDegrade, we constructed an end-to-end attack proving that Raccoon-like exploits can succeed with real data, addressing a gap left by earlier research. As a specific application, we re-examined the "VulnerableV8" configuration of Google Chrome, for which we developed an optimized attack variant using HyperDegrade that is three times more effective than the original. Our investigation into this configuration reveals several contributing vulnerabilities, some of which remain unresolved. Finally, we summarized key lessons learned from this end-to-end attack demonstration to enhance protocol design and security protocols, offering recommendations for protocol designers and vulerability scanners. The source code for HyperDegrade and the end-to-end attack demonstrations used in this evaluation are accessible at https://github.com/CAEIR/PerformanceDegradaion and https://github.com/CAEIR/RealisticE2EAttack, respectively.
An unknotting operation represents a local modification applied to knot diagrams. It is possible to convert any knot diagram into a trivial unknot diagram through a combination of unknotting operations and Reidemeister moves. These operations hold substantial significance in knot theory, particularly for analyzing knot complexity and invariants. Furthermore, they play a crucial role in fields such as biology, chemistry, and physics, where they help investigate the complex entanglements found in strings, organic molecules, and DNA. This paper introduces a novel unknotting operation known as the diagonal move, applicable to both classical and welded knots. We demonstrate that the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move, and 4-move can all be achieved via sequences of diagonal moves. Additionally, we define a distance metric based on the diagonal move and examine its characteristics. Finally, we calculate the diagonal move distances for various famous knots and curves. To facilitate this study, we developed a free software package called Wakd (Wired Knot Diagram), available at https://github.com/YangLi419/Wakd. Our findings indicate that the diagonal move distance for any classical or welded knot is always less than or equal to half its self-linking distance. Moreover, for any sequence of integers 0=n_0<=n_1<=...<=n_r, there exists a classical knot with self-linking distance n_r and diagonal move distance n_r-n_{r-1}. These results confirm that the diagonal move is the optimal measure for classifying classical and welded knots based on their self-linking distances. Among the specific unknotting operations examined in this work, the diagonal move stands out as the most powerful, surpassing the ability of the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move, and 4-move to entangle classical knots and both classical and welded knots to any specified extent. Regarding the diagonal move's implementation, it functions similarly to the Delta-move but differs in how the resulting arcs are reconnected. While the Delta-move alters the embedded arc structure, the diagonal move preserves this structure; instead, it modifies the crossing configuration within an isolated region of the diagram where four arcs meet. Coordination serves as a vital capability in multi-agent systems, enabling the completion of objectives that single agents cannot achieve alone. This study examines how a team of strategic agents selects among multiple tasks within a stochastic framework, specifically focusing on two tasks with randomly distributed and partially observable difficulties. We demonstrate that when prior distributions regarding task difficulty are diffuse, a Nash equilibrium with a straightforward, intuitive linear structure emerges. Conversely, we find that if the prior distribution is not diffuse, an agent's best response to an affine strategy profile may become nonlinear. Furthermore, we present an algorithm capable of efficiently calculating a data-driven Nash equilibrium restricted to the class of affine policies. Finally, we highlight that both the affine policy class and affine best responses perform suboptimally compared to data-driven policies that are not constrained to be affine. By conducting a case study involving a multi-drone system aimed at locating and rescuing a lost individual, we illustrate how varying assumptions about the probability distribution of task difficulty influence the recommended actions and the resulting social utility. The significance of this work lies in the consideration of multi-task selection problems under partial observability, particularly when the task difficulty follows a data-driven distribution derived from observed completion times. This study extends the research of [10], which addressed similar multi-task selection challenges assuming an exponential distribution for task difficulty.

The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by quantum shot noise and ultimately by optical losses within the signal-recycling cavity. This limitation represents a primary barrier to detecting gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers in both current and future detectors, as it remains independent of arm length and the level of injected squeezing. In this study, we propose a sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, derived from a Michelson interferometer by optically linking the end mirrors to form an additional cavity. This configuration creates a triply-coupled cavity system capable of surpassing the loss-induced high-frequency limit inherent to signal-recycled Michelson interferometers. Using parameters comparable to advanced LIGO+, a sloshing-Sagnac design could achieve sevenfold improved sensitivity at 2.5 kHz, or a fourfold increase in signal-to-noise ratio for typical post-merger binary neutron star waveforms. As an evolution of the Michelson architecture, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer offers a viable topology for upgrading current detectors and for future-generation observatories. To evaluate this topology practically, we developed an open-source Python library called PySqueeze, which extends the capabilities of GENCA and LALSIMD to enable frequency-response calculations for complex interferometric layouts. We demonstrate the use of PySqueeze by optimizing a sloshing-Sagnac interferometer with parameters similar to advanced LIGO+ to determine its maximum possible high-frequency sensitivity. Additionally, we assessed a triply-squeezed version of this interferometer, confirming that the benefits from additional squeezing are negated by losses in the squeezed-vacuum lines. Finally, we applied the PySqueeze library to estimate the high-frequency sensitivity limits for geometric-squeezing-sourced limits at both advanced LIGO and third-generation detectors. By extending GENCA and LALSIMD functionalities, PySqueeze serves as an invaluable tool for analyzing the end-to-end sensitivity of sophisticated squeezing-improved interferometers, facilitating the practical implementation of quantum entanglement benefits in next-generation gravitational-wave detectors.
Extra-large scale massive multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems represent a promising solution for delivering ultra-high data rates in environments with high user density. Because the physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays are comparable to the distances separating them from user equipments (UEs), the system experiences spatial non-stationarities and distinct visibility regions (VRs). These factors, combined with high UE density and limited pilot resources, make the design of random access (RA) protocols and scheduling algorithms particularly difficult. This paper introduces a joint RA and scheduling approach called the non-overlapping VR XL-MIMO (NOVR-XL) protocol. This method leverages the unique VRs of individual UEs to enhance RA performance and prioritizes scheduling UEs with non-overlapping VRs within the same payload data pilot resource. Simulation results demonstrate that this proposed scheme yields substantial improvements in sum rate compared to conventional RA methods, while also lowering access latency and overall connectivity performance. Furthermore, the NOVR-XL benefits are even more pronounced in systems with larger array sizes and higher UE densities, making it especially advantageous for extra-large scale massive MIMO deployments. These findings suggest that the NOVR-XL approach is an effective solution for deploying ultra-large scale wireless networks to meet the demands of fifth-generation (5G) and beyond systems.

Although neural language models have largely replaced traditional $N$-gram models due to superior performance, our findings suggest that $N$-grams still yield satisfactory results in many scenarios, effectively capturing significant linguistic knowledge at a low computational cost. Leveraging this insight, we propose training a neural model to predict the residuals between an $N$-gram model and the actual data distribution. In contrast, this work examines subsets of $(N_{p/q})^d$ that are $p/q$-recognisable, meaning they can be recognized by finite automata operating over $(A_p)^d$. Second, we demonstrate that neither the natural ordering relation nor the modulo-$q$ operator are $p/q$-recognisable. Consequently, there has been significant research into fast, approximate iterative methods for matrix inversion accelerated by Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), offering viable alternatives where traditional direct inversion methods are too costly. Existing techniques include the Neumann Series (NS), Newton iteration (NI), Chebyshev Iteration (CI), and Successive Over-Relaxation. This study introduces a novel iterative algorithm derived from the NS, termed "Nested Neumann" (NN). This approach generalizes higher-order iterations of NI and CI by leveraging a computationally efficient iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, dependent on a specified "inception depth." Mathematical analysis confirms that the NN method: (i) converges provided the preconditioning matrix satisfies the spectral norm condition required for NS, (ii) achieves a convergence rate equivalent to an order of (inception depth plus one), and (iii) performs optimally with an inception depth of one or two, contingent upon available RAM. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for NN suitable for massive sparse matrices, accounting for increased computational costs. Crucially, we establish an analytical equivalence between NS and NN (including NI, CI, and higher orders), a finding particularly relevant for mMIMO systems. Finally, the NN method is applicable to positive semi-definite matrices for inversion and can be utilized for any linear system, whether sparse, non-sparse, or complex. Specifically, for sparse matrices, the explicit NN formula serves as a powerful tool; for non-sparse matrices, the implicit NN method acts as an effective counterpart to direct inversion techniques. Regarding direct inversion, we introduce a hybrid variant combining LU decomposition with parallel binary typing (BBT), previously successful with sparse matrices. Comparative results demonstrate that for non-sparse massive matrices, the iterative NN method (with 1000 orders of approximation) is, on average, 2.7 times faster than the direct LU+BBT method using 256 GPUs, and 28 times faster with 64 GPUs. The explicit NN formula for sparse matrices proved even more competitive: it was 31 times faster on 256 GPUs and 36 times faster on 64 GPUs compared to LU+BBT. These findings indicate that the iterative Nested Neumann (NN) method with high-order approximation is a highly viable substitute for direct inversion methods across both sparse and non-sparse massive matrices.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism dependent on rapid gas cooling, potentially active in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks. While the VSI generates turbulence characterized by vigorous vertical motions that can influence dust accumulation and settling, dust evolution itself can suppress this instability. Specifically, as dust grows and settles, it depletes the gas, rendering cooling inefficient in the optically thin outer regions. This study employs linear analysis to quantify how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. We developed a cooling timescale model incorporating dust growth beyond micron scales and size-dependent settling. By integrating this model with linear stability analysis, we identified the "VSI zone" and calculated the maximum growth rate at various radial distances. Our results indicate that both dust growth and settling restrict the VSI zone to the immediate vicinity of the midplane. Consequently, the instability's growth rate diminishes because the vertical shear of rotational velocity—the instability's driving force—is weaker at lower altitudes. In our default model of a 0.01 solar mass disk, dust growth from 10 microns to 1 mm reduces the growth rate by a factor exceeding 10. Ultimately, the suppression of VSI-driven turbulence by dust evolution could accelerate further dust processing in outer disk regions and account for the significant dust settling observed in the HL Tau system. This paper presents an enhanced model of dust evolution in outer protoplanetary disks and establishes a framework for investigating dust-interferenced hydrodynamical instabilities in these environments. To advance our understanding of rapid dust growth in these zones, future efforts should focus on improving models of collisional fragmentation and coagulation, as well as direct numerical simulations capable of resolving individual dust particles.

This report outlines the methodologies that secured 3rd and 4th place in tasks 1 and 2, respectively, at the ISIC 2019 challenge, which aims to diagnose skin cancer using images and metadata. Although the dataset contains nine classes, one is an outlier and absent from the actual data. To address this, we employed an ensemble of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNNs), developed two strategies to manage the missing outlier class, and introduced a simple technique for integrating metadata with image data. We detail each methodology and its parameters throughout this document to ensure replicability. Our results align with previous challenges, and our approaches for detecting the outlier class and leveraging metadata have proven effective. Furthermore, our metadata integration method yielded superior accuracy compared to previous challenges. Finally, our overall performance and strategies for identifying the outlier class achieved the 3rd and 4th ranks for both tasks 1 and 2 at ISIC 2019. Readers can find this paper's preprint at https://arxiv.org/abs/1811/06534 and access the dataset at http://isic-archive.com.
Because of the forward-peaked nature of radiation, lepton colliders operating above a few TeV function effectively as electroweak (EW) boson colliders, implying that EW bosons can be treated as constituents within high-energy leptons. Focusing on muon colliders, we re-examine the validity of $W$ and $Z$ parton distribution functions (PDFs) at leading order for $2\to n$ processes. We systematically analyze universal and quasi-universal power-law and logarithmic corrections that emerge when deriving (polarized) weak boson PDFs in the collinear limit. Furthermore, we survey numerous $2\to n$ processes at center-of-mass energies ranging from 2 to 30 TeV through polarized and unpolarized electroweak boson fusion and scattering. To facilitate this investigation, we present a public implementation of the Effective $W/Z$ and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations—collectively termed the Effective Vector Boson Approximation—within the Monte Carlo event generator \texttt{MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO}. This implementation establishes the foundation for creating matrix-element matching schemes that incorporate EW parton showers and renormalized EW PDFs. In support of this initiative, we also provide specific recommendations regarding the application of $W/Z$ PDFs. Additionally, we offer an implementation of the $V$-Vertex Approximation to enable the investigation of multi-EW-boson vertices and vertices involving EW bosons and other particles. Finally, we establish the Effective Vector Boson Approximation as the appropriate framework for describing $V$n ($V=W,Z$) production in lon-gitude (L) - transverse ($T$) heavy ion collisions, such as those occurring at the future High-Luminosity LHC.
We bring together Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem (1931), Tarski's Undefinability Theorem (1933), Godel-Carnap's Diagonal Lemma (1934), and Rosser's Incompleteness Theorem (1936), which strengthens Godel's first result. These proofs share significant similarities and employ nearly identical techniques. By synthesizing these approaches, we derive an "incompleteness theorem à la Rosser" that applies beyond formal systems to the meta-level, bypassing the limitations imposed by Tarski's Undefinability Theorem. Furthermore, we formulate a "version of the diagonal lemma à la Rosser" operating at the meta-level and an extension of Godel's first incompleteness theorem that includes a specific arithmetic statement akin to Godel's, now called the "Rosser statement," which is comparable to Tarski's Undefinability statement. We also provide a proof of Tarski's theorem at the meta-level and discuss potential extensions of Godel's second incompleteness theorem and the diagonal lemma. All these results rely solely on basic properties of recursive functions and the arithmetic truth predicate, requiring no formal system. Our proofs highlight that Tarski's undefinability statement and Godel's first incompleteness statement (with its arithmetic variant and the Rosser statement) are essentially equivalent (assuming the truth predicate) when derived via the diagonal lemma or its metaphorm, "Wittgenstein's box." Conversely, we demonstrate that Godel's original second incompleteness theorem stands as a distinct result, not merely a consequence of Tarski's undefinability theorem, by constructing a model containing a predicate satisfying Tarski's conditions yet failing to meet Godel's second incompleteness theorem. Finally, we examine the implications of these findings for Hilbert's Program, Tarski's Hierarchy Theorem, Goedel-Lob Theorems concerning modal logic S4 and its LCKR extension, and Rasiowa's Incompleteness Theorem. Despite the length of this introduction, our conclusions offer novel insights, often overlooked even by logicians, providing something new without needing an additional "incompleteness theorem à la Rosser" at the meta-level or a "diagonal lemma à la Rosser" for establishing uniqueness in models of the arithmetic truth predicate, as detailed in the paper's introduction.
Invariant manifolds constitute crucial sets within the stability analysis of dynamical systems. This paper offers a concise overview of invariant sets, presenting findings on the existence of invariant lines and parabolas within planar polynomial systems. Additionally, we establish the criteria required for linear subspaces to remain invariant in fractional-order systems. Furthermore, we highlight a significant result demonstrating that, aside from linear subspaces, no other invariant manifolds exist in such fractional-order systems. The implications of this finding are discussed in detail. Finally, the work concludes by addressing the challenge of proving the invariance of arbitrary sets for these systems. Our discussion underscores that, although this goal appears feasible through the use of characteristic functions, fractional-order dynamics introduce singularities at $t=0$ that obstruct this approach.
This study addresses the inverse problem of identifying a source term within a structural acoustic PDE model, which consists of a two- or three-dimensional interior acoustic wave equation linked to a Kirchhoff plate equation via a boundary interface. For this system, we establish uniqueness and derive stability estimates for the source term using a single boundary measurement of the "structure." The uniqueness proof relies on Carleman estimates, while the stability result is achieved through an observability inequality combined with a compactness/uniqueness argument. Finally, an operator theoretic approach provides the necessary regularity for the initial conditions to attain the desired stability estimate. These theoretical findings are supported by numerical examples that highlight both the inverse problem's characteristics and the efficacy of the proposed stability derivation. By adding a source term to the PDE model, we make this inverse problem relevant to practical applications.
This study examines the coherence of electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino behavior, and dark matter properties within the minimal scoto-seesaw framework. By extending the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw with the minimal dark sector, we establish a physical mechanism for neutrino oscillation lengths: the atmospheric mass scale originates from tree-level seesaw dynamics, whereas the solar scale emerges radiatively through mediation by the dark sector. We pinpoint parameter regions that satisfy theoretical constraints, align with dark matter relic density, and are viable under direct detection limits. Employing two-loop renormalization group equations, we investigate vacuum stability and the consistency of the fundamental dark parity symmetry, confirming all constraints remain valid within our defined parameter space. To enhance the solar mass scale and relieve tension regarding the dark matter relic density, we propose feasible experimental tests via neutrinoless double beta decay, direct dark matter searches, and cosmological observations of the dark matter abundance. Additionally, we identify specific parameters that enable solutions to both the dark matter relic density tension and the Homogenity issue. Finally, we construct an extended sector-1 mixing matrix incorporating one new physics scale ($\Lambda_1$) and one additional mass scale ($M_{\Lambda_2}$) at the dark sector scale, stabilizing the dark matter relic density across a broad range of $f_2$ values; we recommend future direct detection experiments explore this region toconstrain the second new physics scale, $M_{\Lambda_2}$.
